learningObjective: Enumerate boundary conditions that block or complicate operator fusion in a deep-learning compiler.
stem: Which of the following are legitimate fusion-boundary conditions that a deep-learning compiler must respect? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The producer and consumer are placed on different devices (e.g., CPU producer, GPU consumer); crossing the device boundary requires an explicit copy op and cannot be absorbed into a single kernel.
The producer performs an in-place mutation of a tensor that is aliased by another live consumer; fusing across such a mutation would violate the observed side-effect ordering.

The producer and consumer have iteration spaces of very different rank/extent (e.g., a 4D pointwise op followed by a scalar reduction to a 0-D tensor); the compiler must decide whether a common loop nest is expressible.
The producer's output tensor is explicitly marked as a graph output that the caller reads; fusing away its materialization would violate the API contract.
The producer and consumer both use FP32 accumulation; fusing FP32 ops is forbidden because register pressure always grows unboundedly.

The producer is a pointwise op and the consumer is a pointwise op with the same shape; sharing an iteration space and being pure, they must not be fused because pointwise-pointwise fusion is disallowed.

explanation: A, B, D are canonical fusion boundaries. Device boundaries require a data-transfer op and cannot be absorbed into one kernel. In-place mutation with aliased live consumers must preserve the mutation ordering; fusing across it can reorder reads and writes. Explicit graph outputs are contractually observable and cannot be optimized away. C is not a hard boundary — different iteration extents (e.g., pointwise → reduction) are routinely fused when the compiler can express a common nest; it may complicate scheduling but is not a boundary in itself. E is incorrect because FP32 accumulation says nothing about legality; register pressure is a heuristic concern, not a legality one. F is the opposite of the truth: pointwise-pointwise fusion is the most common fusion pattern.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: device boundaries require explicit transfer ops.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: aliased in-place writes constrain reordering.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: differing extents complicate scheduling but do not form a hard boundary; pointwise→reduction is a common fused pattern.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: explicit outputs are observable and cannot be fused away.
optionExplanations.E: Wrong: FP32 usage is not a legality condition; register pressure is a heuristic.
optionExplanations.F: Wrong: pointwise-pointwise fusion is the canonical vertical/horizontal fusion pattern.

assumptions: The IR distinguishes device placement, mutation/aliasing, and graph outputs.
nonImplications: Does not imply that heuristics such as register-pressure limits are illegitimate; they exist but are performance concerns, not legality boundaries.

distractorRationales.C: Confuses scheduling difficulty with a hard legality boundary.
distractorRationales.F: Reverses reality — pointwise-pointwise is the most common fusion.
